..I will be a quiet day across Southeast Arizona 
today as a strong ridge of high pressure centered over the Texas
coastline expands westward across northern Mexico. Southeast 
Arizona will reside on the extreme northwest periphery of this 
expanding ridge, resulting in a few degrees of warming over 
yesterday and afternoon high temperatures generally 2-5 degrees
above normal.

Otherwise, quite a bit of tropical activity across the eastern 
Pacific today, with two hurricanes of note that will have a 
peripheral influence on our weather as early as Sunday but 
more-so Monday and Tuesday. The first feature is defined by the 
NHC at 8 PM MST as Hurricane Odalys, which is a category 3 
system with maximum sustained winds 120 mph near 18.8N/123.6W 
moving N at 4 kts. The second feature defined by the NHC is 
Hurricane Polo, which is a category 5 system with maximum 
sustained winds of 175 mph near 17.4N/110.1W moving WNW at 9 
kts. 

Odalys will move north toward cooler waters this weekend, 
weakening to a tropical storm by 5 PM PDT Sunday afternoon 
near 22.5N/122.5W. As it weakens, it will begin to shear out
in the mid/upper levels ENE toward the Desert Southwest in
response to a strong trough digging south along the California 
coastline. Although this will increase PWATs into the 1.00-1.50
inch range west of Tucson, this will mainly occur in the mid/upper
levels resulting in significant mid and high clouds covering 
Southeast Arizona along with just enough dynamics to result in a
few light showers west of Tucson Sunday afternoon/evening. The 
lower-levels will remain dry Sunday afternoon and evening, so 
it will look like one of those dreary, thick-virga kinda days
with a few gusts to 30 mph near the downdrafts.

With regards to the stronger Hurricane Polo, this feature will 
provide our neck of the woods with a moist tropical airmass.
Monday into Tuesday. Polo is progged to move northwest today
with the westward expansion if the subtropical ridge. As the 
ridge begins to retreat east Sunday in response to the trough 
digging south along the West Coast, Polo will move north Sunday,
then eventually recurve to the NE and weaken to a category 1
between the Baja Spur and tip of the Baja by5 PM PDT Monday
afternoon. This track will help push tropical moisture northward  
up the Gulf of California Sunday and across all of southern 
Arizona Monday and Tuesday. The 26/00Z GEFS and ECMWF ensemble 
means still indicate a plume of moist PWATs 2.5-3.0 standard 
deviations above normal across Southeast Arizona by 29/00Z 
Monday afternoon.

As I mentioned yesterday, although we will see a deep plume of 
tropical moisture across our neck of the woods with the
peripheral assist by Polo, it is important to note that the 
remains of Polo are NOT expected to impact us directly. The 
official track by the NHC has Polo holding together as a 
tropical storm south of us in east-central Sonora Mexico (near 
the Sonora/Chihuahua border) at 5 PM PDT Tuesday afternoon. 

Our precipitation event will be a synoptic system utilizing the
tropical moisture available across the area. That trough digging
south along the California coastline will produce a strong
upper-low centered near the California Bight 29/00Z Monday 
afternoon, then track this feature across Arizona Tuesday and
Tuesday night. Given the deep moisture in place, this feature 
will result in widespread showers and thunderstorms across 
Southeast Arizona...especially Monday night and Tuesday. Modest
deformation in the flow aloft Monday will support mainly light 
to moderate intensity rainfall with pockets of heavy rain, with 
the potential for more widespread moderate to heavy rainfall 
Tuesday with stronger dynamics along and near the trough axis.
Current thinking is that pcpn will be near the NBM 50th
percentile with maximum values near the 75th percentile. My
expectation then is; Monday (1/4 - 1/2 inch with localized amts
up to 3/4 inch psbl), Monday night (1/2 - 3/4 inch with
localized amts up to 1 inch psbl), Tuesday (1/2 - 1 inch with 
localized amts up to 1.5 inches psbl). Although rainfall rates
may not be as impressive as we see during the heart of the
Monsoon, this rainfall may be more widespread and become
problematic with time as rainfall runoff struggles to drain into
normally dry washes, roadway dips and other low-lying areas. The
WPC has SE AZ in the slight risk category for rainfall to exceed
flash flood guidance both Monday and Tuesday. This seems prudent,
and we may eventually need to consider issuing a Flash Flood 
Watch for this period.

Storms on Tuesday and Tuesday night may get a little frisky with
strong 0-6km bulk shear present. This will bring about the 
potential for a few mini-supercells to be embedded within the 
widespread storm activity. Lingering instability and moisture 
will be present Wednesday for additional shower activity, but
